title: Somatic cells kept their cognitive repertoire and scaled it to anatomical goals

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Somatic cells kept their cognitive repertoire and scaled it to anatomical goals

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The authors argue that somatic cells did not lose their ancestral cognitive and computational capabilities when they became part of multicellular bodies, but scaled them up to pursue larger anatomical goals.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Pio-Lopez L 2023, The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis › Discussion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But somatic cells did not lose their cognitive repertoire and computational capabilities during their transitions to multicellularity or in becoming part of metazoan swarms (bodies): they scaled them to pursue larger anatomical goals [4].

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Pio-Lopez L, Bischof J, LaPalme JV, Levin M, “The scaling of goals from cellular to anatomical homeostasis: an evolutionary simulation, experiment and analysis”, Interface focus (2023), doi:10.1098/rsfs.2022.0072; section “Discussion”. Scope: Metazoan somatic cells and their unicellular ancestors

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-goals-19: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.32

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Comparative cell biology can test continuity of particular pathways or behaviours, but the claim as stated packages those observations into a broad cognitive historical interpretation. Plausible outcomes remain compatible with non-cognitive descriptions, so it lacks a decisive empirical criterion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: No observation uniquely distinguishes retention and scaling of an ancestral 'cognitive repertoire' from evolution of multicellular regulatory mechanisms unless specific ancestral capacities, homologous mechanisms, and quantitative collective goals are defined.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ancestral states are not directly observed.

Cognitive repertoire and anatomical goals are framework-dependent.

Mechanistic continuity does not distinguish retention from exaptation.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The historical and cognitive wording does not add an observation beyond multicellular use of conserved cellular control loops. Any dataset of channel genes, regeneration, or learning in unicells can be described without a retained cognitive repertoire. The claim is therefore not separated from its non-cognitive rival by existing data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: A non-cognitive description, in which the same ion channels, stresses, and gene-regulatory loops implement physiological homeostasis at cell and tissue scale, predicts the same developmental and regenerative observations. No public measurement separates retained ancestral cognition scaled to anatomical goals from that physiological description, so there is no confirming or refuting outcome.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Comparative presence of ancient cell-biological machinery does not decide whether that machinery is cognition.

Cognitive repertoire and anatomical goals have several contested operationalizations.
